<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a well-designed follow-up. It answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents: hours are now measured from system logs, the mediation test was registered before the outcomes were available, and the treatment of the Halden survivors is candid. The arithmetic is correct. The main problems are in how the decline in the effect and the mediation result are interpreted, plus one inconsistency in the meetings data.

## 1. Arithmetic: correct

- **Timesheet measure.** 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8%.
- **Log measure.** 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers.** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a 13.4% cut in hours, and 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118, so +11.8%.
- **Meetings difference-in-differences.** Treated offices fell 3.5 hours and control offices 0.2, a net difference of 3.3 hours. That matches the 3.3-hour gap the nine-month report found at month six.

## 2. The Summary overstates the decline by switching measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% was measured with timesheets and 8.5% with system logs. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, as the body text correctly says. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" falls between the two:

- 12.5 → 9.8 is a decline of about 22%.
- 12.5 → 8.5 is a decline of about 32%.

The Summary should report both measures separately, and Section 5 should say which comparison it means.

## 3. The control offices' meeting audit was contamination, and the decay interpretation ignores it

In month 15, two control offices cut their meetings and saw a 4.1% rise in output per hour. The report treats this as a side observation. It also matters for the main estimate:

- **It lowers the measured treatment effect after month 15.** The difference-in-differences compares treated offices with control. If two of the seven control offices improved, the treatment effect shrinks even if treated offices held steady. Some of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect control offices improving, not the treatment fading.
- **The fix is straightforward.** Report treated and control trends separately. Also re-estimate the effect excluding the two audit offices, or excluding the period after month 15.
- **It may be spillover from the trial itself.** Control offices "on their own initiative" adopting the very practice the trial highlighted is a likely case of contamination, which is the thing office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

## 4. The control-office meeting figures don't add up

The two audit offices cut meetings from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, a drop of 2.1 hours each. Averaged across seven control offices, that alone would lower the control mean by about 0.6 hours. Yet the control mean moved only from 7.2 to 7.0. For both figures to hold, the other five control offices must have *increased* meeting time by about 0.5 hours each. That's possible, but it needs to be stated. Otherwise one of the figures is wrong.

## 5. Where did the baseline meeting data come from?

The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six, at managers' request. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. If these were retrieved retrospectively from calendar systems, the report should say so, and say how complete the records are.

## 6. The mediation analysis: "confirms" is too strong

**The test isn't independent of the data that suggested it.** It was registered at month 11, after the exploratory finding. It uses 24 months of office data, which include the first nine months that generated the hypothesis. That makes it a pre-specified analysis, not an independent replication. The "larger sample of office-months" also doesn't add independent units: there are still 14 clusters.

**Part of the meetings pathway may be accounting, not behaviour.** The answer depends on whether "active log-in time" includes time spent in meetings:

- **If it does:** total hours fell about 4.5 a week, and meetings account for 3.3 of that. Output per hour then rises largely because meeting time no longer counts in the denominator. That is still a useful finding, since it shows *where* the hours cut came from, but it isn't evidence that staff worked more effectively.
- **If it doesn't:** the meetings pathway means fewer meetings made case work itself more productive, for example through less fragmented time. That would be a stronger and more interesting claim.

The report needs to define the log measure, because the two readings support different conclusions.

**The causal assumptions carry a lot of weight.** The Limitations section concedes that meeting time wasn't randomised. Three further points should be addressed:

- Meetings and fatigue are probably linked, since fewer meetings may reduce fatigue. The 47% and 18% shares therefore depend on how the two pathways are modelled together.
- Shares of a modest total effect are statistically unstable.
- The report doesn't say whether the confidence intervals were corrected for the small number of clusters. I raised this for the nine-month results, and it still applies.

"Survives a registered test" is fair. "Confirms" in the Summary is not.

## 7. The Halden follow-up

- **More self-selection.** Of the 23 organisations contacted, 14 responded. That is a third layer of selection, after the withdrawals during the pilot and the decision to continue.
- **Not all the reverters were coverage-bound.** The Summary groups all three reverters as having "client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited client deadlines, and the meta-analysis's coding would class marketing as *discretionary*. So one of the three reverters was in the kind of work that supposedly suits reduced hours. That deserves mention, not absorption into the coverage story.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** With no control group, two years of general trends could push output in either direction. "Probably biased upward" is defensible; "upper bound" is not.
- **Output measures.** If any of the continuing organisations use billable hours as their output measure, the earlier concern applies: billable hours are partly an input and fall automatically when hours are cut.
- **A missed opportunity on attrition.** Okafor, an author of the original Halden paper, is a co-author here. Varga and Holm reported that seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, contrary to the working paper. This report could have addressed that discrepancy and doesn't.

## 8. Section 5 is mostly fair

- **On Varga and Holm.** The response is well judged. It credits what they got right and shows that their own recommended standards still yield a gain of +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8).
- **On the meta-analysis.** The revelation that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours is decisive. It confirms the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" claim was unsupported.
- **A small slip.** The report repeats the comment's "month ten" for when energy would return to baseline. The comment's own straight-line extrapolation gives about month 8.7. This doesn't change the rebuttal.

## 9. Items still not reported

- **Backlog and case age.** These still aren't reported. With 24 months of data, they can now show whether output was kept up by letting cases build toward their statutory deadlines.
- **Sick days.** The fall of 27% may still partly reflect fewer scheduled days, and no confidence interval is given.
- **Resignations.** The figures are still treated-versus-control levels, without a difference-in-differences estimate or an interval.

## Where the evidence now stands

Across the five documents:

- **Per-hour gains are real but modest.** In the cleanest evidence, randomised case-processing offices with system-measured hours, the gain is about 8–10% at two years. That is well below the 20%+ from early pilots, but not zero.
- **Output per worker:** roughly held in discretionary work, with a slight shortfall. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours cost service unless staff are added, and the Varden county ended that arm for this reason.
- **The gain has probably faded somewhat.** How much is uncertain, partly because of the contamination of control offices.
- **A large share of the gain appears to come from cutting meetings.** It's unclear whether that is a behavioural effect or an accounting one. It's also unclear whether reorganising work without cutting hours would capture it. No study yet has the arm that would answer this: an office that reorganises without reducing hours.

I can turn this into a referee report, or draft a fuller synthesis across all five documents.
